questions.text: Every strengthening mechanism in this course works by:

statements.text: impeding dislocation motion
adding obstacles the dislocation must overcome
reducing the number of dislocations
raising the applied stress needed for slip

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 4 correct. Item 3 is the opposite — deformation *raises* dislocation density.
questions.concise: All mechanisms work by impeding dislocation motion / adding obstacles / raising the required stress — but deformation *raises* dislocation density, never reduces it.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: every mechanism impedes dislocation motion. That is the definition.
- Item 2 — TRUE: each puts a specific obstacle in the dislocation's path (Q2).
- Item 3 — FALSE: deformation *increases* dislocation density (10⁶ → 10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻², Ch. 5
  Q43). Reducing density would *soften* the metal (that is what recovery does).
- Item 4 — TRUE: the practical consequence is a higher applied stress for slip.

Item 3 is the false member. The organising idea of the whole chapter: **strengthening = making
dislocation motion harder.** Anything that removes dislocations works the other way.

questions.text: Match the mechanism to the obstacle it puts in the dislocation's way.
questions.keyExplanation: 1-b (dislocations), 2-a (boundaries), 3-d (solute), 4-c (particles). Learn this mapping — it is the organising idea of the whole chapter.
questions.concise: work hardening→other dislocations · grain refinement→boundaries · solid solution→solute atoms · precipitation→second-phase particles.
questions.detailed:
| Mechanism | Obstacle |
|---|---|
| Strain (work) hardening | other dislocations (forest dislocations) |
| Grain refinement (Hall–Petch) | grain boundaries |
| Solid-solution strengthening | solute atoms (their strain fields) |
| Precipitation (age) hardening | second-phase particles |

Learn this mapping cold — it is the organising idea of the entire chapter. Once you have it,
every "which mechanism uses which obstacle" question is instant recall.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are among the four classic strengthening mechanisms?

statements.text: Strain (work) hardening
Grain refinement
Solid-solution strengthening
Precipitation (age) hardening

questions.keyExplanation: All four are the classic mechanisms.
questions.concise: All four are the classic strengthening mechanisms.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: strain (work) hardening.
- Item 2 — TRUE: grain refinement (Hall–Petch).
- Item 3 — TRUE: solid-solution strengthening.
- Item 4 — TRUE: precipitation (age) hardening.

All four are correct — a genuine "all are correct" case with no false member. The number to
remember is **four**. If a question ever offers a fifth "mechanism", be suspicious — deformation
processing and heat treatment achieve their effects *through* these four, not alongside them.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about work hardening is/are correct?

statements.text: Plastic deformation multiplies dislocation density via Frank–Read sources.
Density rises from ~10⁶ cm⁻² (annealed) to 10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻² (heavily cold worked).
Dislocations cut across each other's slip planes (forest dislocations), tangle and pile up.
Flow stress *falls* with increasing strain.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is false — flow stress *rises* with strain.
questions.concise: Frank–Read multiplication, 10⁶→10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻², forest cutting/tangling — but flow stress *rises* with strain.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: Frank–Read sources multiply dislocations during plastic deformation.
- Item 2 — TRUE: density rises from ~10⁶ cm⁻² (annealed) to 10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻² (heavily cold worked).
- Item 3 — TRUE: dislocations on intersecting ("forest") slip planes cut across each other,
  tangle and pile up — each intersection is an obstacle to further motion.
- Item 4 — FALSE: flow stress *rises* with strain. If it fell, the deformation would be
  unstable and the material would have no strength left.

Item 4 is a direct reversal of the defining feature of work hardening.

questions.text: The three-stage work-hardening curve for an FCC single crystal consists of:

options.label: a
options.text: Stage I easy glide (single slip) → Stage II multiple slip, linear hardening → Stage III dynamic recovery, parabolic

options.label: b
options.text: Stage I parabolic → Stage II easy glide → Stage III linear

questions.keyExplanation: Easy glide → multiple slip/linear → dynamic recovery/parabolic.
questions.concise: Easy glide → multiple slip/linear → dynamic recovery/parabolic.
questions.detailed:
The three-stage FCC single-crystal work-hardening curve:
```
Stage I — easy glide:     single slip system active, low hardening rate
Stage II — linear:        multiple slip, forest intersections, steep linear hardening
Stage III — parabolic:    dynamic recovery (climb + cross-slip) offsets hardening,
                          giving a flattening, parabolic curve
```
- (b) scrambles the order.
- (c), (d) understate the number of stages.
Stage I is easy because only one system runs; Stage II is hard because systems intersect; Stage
III flattens because recovery starts winning.

questions.text: Polycrystalline metals skip Stage I (easy glide) entirely because:

statements.text: grain constraints force multiple slip systems active from the very first increment of strain
each grain is constrained by its neighbours
they have no dislocations
Stage I only occurs in HCP metals

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2 correct. Item 3 is nonsense; item 4 is false (Stage I is a single-crystal FCC phenomenon).
questions.concise: Grain constraints force multiple slip from the first increment of strain — items 3 and 4 are false/nonsense.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: grain constraints force multiple slip systems active from the very first
  increment of strain.
- Item 2 — TRUE: each grain is constrained by its neighbours (compatibility at boundaries).
- Item 3 — FALSE: polycrystals obviously contain dislocations; that is what deforms them.
- Item 4 — FALSE: Stage I (easy glide) is a *single-crystal FCC* phenomenon — it is not
  specific to HCP, and polycrystals of any structure skip it.

Items 1 and 2 are really the same fact stated twice (constraint → multiple slip), which is why
they belong together in the answer.

questions.text: Increasing the test temperature:

statements.text: activates dynamic recovery (climb and cross-slip) faster
lets dislocations annihilate or rearrange into lower-energy configurations (e.g. cell walls)
therefore *reduces* the hardening rate and the peak achievable strength
increases the hardening rate

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 states the opposite of the temperature effect.
questions.concise: Higher T accelerates climb/cross-slip recovery → dislocations annihilate/rearrange → lower hardening rate and lower peak strength.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: temperature activates dynamic recovery (climb needs vacancy diffusion, which
  is thermally activated — Ch. 5 Q27).
- Item 2 — TRUE: dislocations annihilate (opposite signs) or rearrange into lower-energy
  configurations such as cell walls/subgrain boundaries.
- Item 3 — TRUE: recovery offsets hardening, so the hardening *rate* and the achievable peak
  strength both fall.
- Item 4 — FALSE: states the exact opposite of item 3.

Items 3 and 4 are direct opposites, so any option containing item 4 is wrong.

questions.text: Solute (composition) affects work hardening by:

options.label: a
options.text: raising the base flow stress and slowing recovery, raising the whole curve

questions.keyExplanation: Solute raises flow stress and slows recovery.
questions.concise: Solute raises the baseline flow stress and slows recovery → whole curve sits higher.
questions.detailed:
Solute atoms strengthen in two ways here:
1. they raise the base (zero-strain) flow stress by solid-solution strengthening (§7.3);
2. they **drag/impede recovery** — solute atmospheres pin dislocations and slow climb and
   cross-slip, so the dynamic-recovery stage starts later.

Both effects push the stress–strain curve upward. Options (b), (c), (d) all state the reverse
or deny any effect.

questions.text: Finer grain size causes a metal to:

options.label: a
options.text: start hardening from a higher baseline stress and generally work harden faster initially

options.label: b
options.text: start hardening from a lower baseline

questions.keyExplanation: Fine grains → higher baseline, faster initial hardening (more pile-ups sooner).
questions.concise: Fine grains → higher baseline (Hall–Petch) and faster initial hardening (more pile-ups sooner).
questions.detailed:
A finer grain size means:
- a **higher starting stress** because of Hall–Petch (more boundaries, Q12);
- a **faster initial hardening rate** because more pile-ups build up per unit strain and
  boundaries multiply the obstacles.
- (b), (c), (d) all contradict this.
This is a nice cross-chapter link: grain refinement (a strengthening mechanism in its own right)
also *changes the shape* of the work-hardening curve.

questions.assertion: Stage III of the work-hardening curve is parabolic.
questions.reason: Stage III is governed by dynamic recovery — climb and cross-slip let dislocations annihilate or rearrange into lower-energy cell structures, progressively offsetting the hardening.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — dynamic recovery is exactly why Stage III is parabolic.
questions.concise: Dynamic recovery (climb + cross-slip → cell structures) is exactly why Stage III is parabolic.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: Stage III of the work-hardening curve is parabolic (flattening), not linear.
- R is TRUE: Stage III is governed by dynamic recovery — climb and cross-slip let dislocations
  annihilate or rearrange into lower-energy cell structures, progressively offsetting the
  hardening.

R correctly explains A. The shape of the curve is set by the *competition* between hardening
(dislocation multiplication) and recovery (annihilation/rearrangement). In Stage III recovery
catches up progressively, so the curve bends over into a parabola rather than continuing linearly.

questions.text: The empirical strain-hardening relation is:

options.label: a
options.text: σ = Kεⁿ, where n is the strain-hardening exponent (0 for perfectly plastic, up to ~0.5 for highly hardenable metals)

options.label: d
options.text: τ = σ cos φ cos λ

questions.keyExplanation: σ = Kεⁿ. [P2] — do not confuse with Hall–Petch or Schmid.
questions.concise: σ = Kεⁿ — the Hollomon relation.
questions.detailed:
```
σ = K εⁿ
K = strength coefficient
n = strain-hardening exponent, 0 ≤ n ≤ ~0.5
```
- n = 0 → perfectly plastic (no hardening).
- n ≈ 0.5 → highly hardenable metal (large hardening response).
- (b) σ = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2) is **Hall–Petch** (Q12, this chapter).
- (c) σ = Eε is **Hooke's law** (elastic, Ch. 6).
- (d) τ = σ cos φ cos λ is **Schmid's law** (Ch. 6 Q14).
**[P2] the three-way confusion:** three famous power-law-looking equations from three different
chapters. Know which belongs where — this is a favourite discriminator.

questions.text: The Hall–Petch equation is:
questions.keyExplanation: σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2). Note the **negative** half power.
questions.concise: σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2) — note the **negative** half power.
questions.detailed:
```
σ_y = σ₀ + k_y · d^(−1/2)   =   σ₀ + k_y / √d
```
- (b) d^(+1/2) would make yield strength *fall* as grains get finer — the opposite of the effect.
- (c) σ₀ d² + k_y is not the relation.
- (d) is the strain-hardening relation (Q11).
The negative half-power is the whole point: **smaller d → larger d^(−1/2) → higher σ_y.**

questions.text: In the Hall–Petch equation, σ₀ is:

options.label: a
options.text: the friction stress opposing dislocation motion in a single crystal (lattice + solute contributions)

questions.keyExplanation: σ₀ = friction stress. [P2]
questions.concise: σ₀ = friction stress (lattice + solute drag), the d → ∞ intercept.
questions.detailed:
σ₀ is the *athermal lattice friction stress* — the stress needed to move a
dislocation through a perfect, solute-containing lattice with no grain boundaries at all. It is
the intercept of the Hall–Petch plot at d^(−1/2) = 0 (i.e. an infinitely large grain).
- (b) k_y is the locking parameter (Q14).
- (c) d is the grain diameter (Q15).
- (d) the applied stress is σ_y, the left-hand side.
σ₀, k_y and d is a **three-way confusion risk** — see Q14 and Q15.

questions.text: In the Hall–Petch equation, k_y is:

options.label: a
options.text: the locking parameter — how effectively boundaries block slip transmission

questions.keyExplanation: k_y = locking parameter. [P2]
questions.concise: k_y = locking parameter (boundary strength), the slope.
questions.detailed:
k_y measures **how effectively grain boundaries block slip transfer** — the
slope of the σ_y vs d^(−1/2) line. A material with a large k_y gains more strengthening per unit
refinement (e.g. low-temperature BCC metals have large k_y; FCC metals have smaller k_y).
- (b) σ₀ is the friction stress (Q13).
- (c) d is the grain diameter (Q15).
- (d) the strain-hardening exponent is n (Q11).

questions.text: In the Hall–Petch equation, d is:
questions.keyExplanation: d = average grain diameter. [P2] — σ₀, k_y, d is a three-way confusion risk.
questions.concise: d = average grain diameter.
questions.detailed:
d is the **average grain diameter** (equivalent-sphere or intercept diameter).
- (b) dislocation density is ρ (units cm⁻²).
- (c) the Burgers vector magnitude is b.
- (d) the diffusion coefficient is D (Ch. 8).
Q13/Q14/Q15 together form a three-way symbol-recognition test. A fast fix: say the equation out
loud — *"yield equals friction stress plus locking parameter times one over root d."* The words
name the symbols.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about grain refinement is/are correct?

statements.text: It is the **only** strengthening method that improves strength and toughness simultaneously.
All other mechanisms trade ductility for strength.
Finer grains mean more grain-boundary area per unit volume, obstructing dislocation pile-up and slip transfer.
Grain refinement reduces toughness.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 contradicts item 1. [P1]
questions.concise: Grain refinement is the ONLY mechanism improving strength AND toughness together; item 4 directly contradicts item 1.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: it is the **only** strengthening method that improves strength and toughness
  simultaneously. This is the single most quoted one-liner in the chapter.
- Item 2 — TRUE: all other mechanisms (work hardening, solid solution, precipitation) trade
  ductility/toughness for strength.
- Item 3 — TRUE: finer grains → more grain-boundary area per unit volume → more barriers to
  pile-up and slip transfer.
- Item 4 — FALSE: grain refinement *raises* toughness (finer grain → higher Charpy impact
  energy, lower ductile–brittle transition temperature). It directly contradicts item 1.

Item 4 is the false member. **The fact to never lose:** *Hall–Petch is the only mechanism that
raises strength **and** toughness together* — a favourite exam one-liner.

questions.assertion: A Hall–Petch plot of σ_y versus d^(−1/2) is a straight line.
questions.reason: Yield strength scales linearly with d^(−1/2), so finer grain size (larger d^(−1/2)) always means a stronger metal.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — σ_y is linear in d^(−1/2).
questions.concise: σ_y is linear in d^(−1/2), so finer grain (larger d^(−1/2)) always means stronger.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: a plot of σ_y against d^(−1/2) is a straight line — that is the definition of the
  Hall–Petch relationship.
- R is TRUE: yield strength scales linearly with d^(−1/2), so larger d^(−1/2) (smaller d) gives
  a higher σ_y.

R correctly explains A — the linearity *is* the content of R. (Note the standard caveat: the
relationship eventually breaks down for nanometre grains, but within the normal metallurgical
range it is linear.)

questions.assertion: Smaller grains require a higher applied stress to transmit slip across the boundary.
questions.reason: A longer pile-up (which needs a *larger* grain to accumulate more dislocations) concentrates more stress for the same applied load; so a small grain, which cannot hold a long pile-up, needs more applied stress to reach the stress needed to trigger slip in the neighbour.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — this is the standard (correct) causal chain for Hall–Petch.
questions.concise: A small grain can't hold a long pile-up, so more applied stress is needed to reach the stress that triggers slip in the neighbour.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: smaller grains need a higher applied stress to transmit slip across the boundary.
- R is TRUE: the stress concentration at the head of a pile-up scales with the number of
  dislocations in it. A **longer** pile-up (which needs a **larger** grain to accommodate it)
  concentrates more stress for the same applied load. So a **small** grain, which cannot hold a
  long pile-up, needs a **larger applied stress** to build up enough head stress to trigger slip
  in the neighbouring grain.

R correctly explains A. This is the standard causal chain behind Hall–Petch, and it links
directly to Ch. 5 Q44 (pile-up head stress ≈ n × applied stress). Walk the chain:
```
small grain → cannot hold many dislocations → short pile-up → weak head stress
→ must raise applied stress to compensate → higher σ_y
```

questions.text: Halving the grain diameter d changes d^(−1/2) by a factor of:
questions.keyExplanation: d → d/2 gives d^(−1/2) → √2 × larger.
questions.concise: d → d/2 makes d^(−1/2) grow by √2.
questions.detailed:
```
before:  d^(−1/2)
after:   (d/2)^(−1/2) = d^(−1/2) × 2^(1/2) = √2 × d^(−1/2)
```
So halving the grain diameter increases d^(−1/2) by a factor of **√2 ≈ 1.414**.
- (b) 2 would be the factor for 1/d.
- (c) 4 would be the factor for 1/d².
- (d) 1/√2 would be the factor for *doubling* d.
**Consequence:** halving grain size adds only k_y(√2 − 1) ≈ 0.41 k_y to the yield strength —
a modest, *square-root-law* gain, not a doubling.

questions.text: Grain boundaries strengthen because:

statements.text: they are barriers to dislocation motion
dislocations pile up against them, creating a stress concentration at the pile-up head
that stress concentration is what triggers slip in the neighbouring grain
they reduce the dislocation density to zero

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is false.
questions.concise: Boundaries are barriers → pile-ups form → head stress triggers slip next door; they do not reduce dislocation density to zero.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: grain boundaries are barriers to dislocation motion (lattice mismatch across them).
- Item 2 — TRUE: dislocations pile up against them, creating a stress concentration at the
  pile-up head.
- Item 3 — TRUE: that stress concentration is what triggers slip in the neighbouring grain.
- Item 4 — FALSE: boundaries do **not** reduce dislocation density to zero. (Grain boundaries
  are actually good *sinks* for dislocations during recovery — they absorb them — but they are
  certainly not zero-density regions, and absorbing dislocations would be a *softening* effect.)

Items 1–3 form the complete Hall–Petch mechanism; item 4 is an invented extreme.

questions.text: Grain refinement is achieved industrially by:

statements.text: rapid cooling (more nuclei, finer grains)
adding grain-refining inoculants
recrystallisation of a heavily cold-worked structure
slow furnace cooling

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 gives *coarse* grains.
questions.concise: Rapid cooling, inoculants and recrystallisation all refine grains; slow cooling coarsens them.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: rapid cooling → more nuclei → finer grains (Ch. 3 Q16–Q18).
- Item 2 — TRUE: grain-refining inoculants provide heterogeneous nucleation sites (Ch. 3 Q13).
- Item 3 — TRUE: recrystallisation of a heavily cold-worked structure nucleates many new
  strain-free fine grains (§7.5).
- Item 4 — FALSE: slow furnace cooling gives *coarse* grains — growth dominates over
  nucleation. This is the opposite of refinement.
Item 4 is the false member, and it is a genuine industrial practice (slow cool for coarse
grains) misfiled as a refining method.

questions.text: Solid-solution strengthening works because:

options.label: a
options.text: dissolved solute atoms distort the lattice, and their local strain field interacts elastically with a dislocation's own strain field

options.label: b
options.text: solute atoms reduce the dislocation density

options.label: c
options.text: solute atoms increase the grain size

options.label: d
options.text: solute atoms raise the melting point only

questions.keyExplanation: Strain-field interaction between solute and dislocation.
questions.concise: Solute strain field ↔ dislocation strain field elastic interaction.

questions.text: Which statement(s) contrast substitutional and interstitial solute strengthening?

statements.text: Substitutional solutes produce a roughly symmetric, spherical strain field (size misfit) plus a modulus misfit.
Interstitial solutes sit in an already-tight void and produce a much larger, asymmetric strain field.
An asymmetric field interacts far more strongly with an edge dislocation's own asymmetric (tension/compression) field.
Interstitial and substitutional solutes are equally potent per atomic percent.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — interstitials are far *more* potent. [P2]
questions.concise: Substitutional = roughly symmetric strain field; interstitial = larger, asymmetric field matching the edge dislocation's asymmetric field; they are NOT equally potent.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: substitutional solutes produce a roughly symmetric, spherical strain field
  (size misfit) plus a modulus misfit.
- Item 2 — TRUE: interstitial solutes sit in an already-tight void and produce a much larger,
  asymmetric strain field (Ch. 2 Q43 — carbon is larger than every void in iron).
- Item 3 — TRUE: an asymmetric field interacts far more strongly with an edge dislocation's own
  asymmetric (tension/compression) field — the match is geometric as well as energetic.
- Item 4 — FALSE: interstitials are **far more potent** per atomic percent — this is exactly
  why tiny amounts of C and N harden steel so much.

Item 4 reverses the truth. **The chain:** bigger field + asymmetric shape + matching asymmetry
= much stronger interaction = more strengthening per atom.

questions.text: Small amounts of interstitial carbon or nitrogen strengthen iron far more, per atomic percent, than substitutional alloying elements. Which statement(s) explain(s) this?

statements.text: Interstitial solutes produce a larger strain field.
The interstitial field is asymmetric, matching the edge dislocation's asymmetric field.
Interstitial atoms are always larger than the host atoms.
Interstitial solutes dissolve without any lattice strain.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2 correct. Item 3 is not the stated reason; item 4 is false (interstitials *always* cost strain energy — carbon is larger than every void). [P1]
questions.concise: Larger strain field and asymmetric field matching the edge dislocation — items 3 and 4 are both false.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: interstitial solutes produce a larger strain field.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the interstitial field is asymmetric, matching the edge dislocation's
  asymmetric tension/compression field.
- Item 3 — FALSE: interstitial atoms are *smaller* than the host atoms (that is why they fit
  in the gaps at all) — though still larger than the voids themselves. The statement "always
  larger than the host atoms" is false and, in any case, is not the *reason* for the potency.
- Item 4 — FALSE: interstitials **always** cost lattice strain energy — carbon (0.08 nm) is
  larger than every available void in iron (Ch. 2 Q43). Dissolving without strain is impossible.

Items 3 and 4 are both false, and both would *remove* the very mechanism that causes the
strengthening. This is a [P1] question where the false members are physically self-defeating.

questions.text: Strengthening from solid solution:

statements.text: increases with solute concentration
but *sub-linearly* — doubling solute content less than doubles the strengthening
because solute atoms increasingly interact with each other as concentration rises
is independent of concentration

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is false.
questions.concise: Strengthening rises with concentration but sub-linearly, because solute–solute interactions start to matter.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: strengthening increases with solute concentration.
- Item 2 — TRUE: but **sub-linearly** — doubling solute content less than doubles the
  strengthening.
- Item 3 — TRUE: because at higher concentration solute atoms increasingly interact with *each
  other* (their strain fields overlap and partly cancel), so each extra atom contributes less.
- Item 4 — FALSE: directly contradicts item 1.

Item 4 is the false member. The sub-linear (often square-root-of-concentration) dependence is
why solid solution alone cannot reach the strengths that precipitation hardening can.

questions.text: Solid-solution strengthening generally scales with:

options.label: a
options.text: the size mismatch between solute and solvent atoms — bigger misfit, bigger strain field, bigger strengthening

questions.keyExplanation: Size mismatch dominates.
questions.concise: Size mismatch dominates.
questions.detailed:
Solid-solution strengthening scales primarily with the **atomic size mismatch**
(Δr/r), because a size misfit produces the largest strain field. A secondary contribution comes
from the **modulus mismatch** (ΔG/G).
- (b), (c), (d) are secondary or unrelated — electronegativity and valence matter for *whether
  a solution forms* (Hume-Rothery, Ch. 4), and density is irrelevant to strengthening.

questions.assertion: Carbon and nitrogen are far more potent strengtheners of iron than substitutional alloying elements such as chromium or nickel, atom for atom.
questions.reason: Their large, asymmetric strain fields couple strongly to the edge dislocation's own asymmetric tension/compression field.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true.
questions.concise: Large, asymmetric C/N strain fields couple strongly to the edge dislocation's own asymmetric field.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: carbon and nitrogen are far more potent strengtheners of iron, atom for atom, than
  substitutional alloying elements such as chromium or nickel.
- R is TRUE: their large, asymmetric strain fields couple strongly to the edge dislocation's
  own asymmetric tension/compression field.

R correctly explains A. The potency is not about size alone — it is about the **shape match**
between an asymmetric solute field and an asymmetric dislocation field. A substitutional solute
with a symmetric field cannot make that match, so it couples less strongly.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the *mechanism* of solid-solution strengthening is/are correct?

statements.text: Both size (misfit) and modulus (misfit) contributions are involved.
Solute atoms interact with both edge and screw dislocations, but only moderately with either.
It is the same general idea as the Cottrell-atmosphere pinning of Chapter 6, generalised from carbon-in-iron to any solute.
It works by reducing dislocation mobility to zero.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 overstates — solute *hinders*, it does not stop, dislocation motion.
questions.concise: Size + modulus misfit, moderate interaction with both edge and screw, and it is the generalisation of the Cottrell-atmosphere idea — but it hinders rather than stops motion.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: both size (misfit) and modulus (misfit) contributions are involved.
- Item 2 — TRUE: solute atoms interact with both edge and screw dislocations, but only
  moderately with either — solute strengthening is a *modest* effect compared to precipitation.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it is the same general idea as the Cottrell atmosphere of Ch. 6, generalised
  from carbon-in-iron to *any* solute in *any* solvent.
- Item 4 — FALSE: it works by **reducing** dislocation mobility, not to zero. Mobility is
  hindered (more stress needed), not eliminated — if mobility were zero the metal could not
  deform at all and would be infinitely strong.

Item 4 overstates the effect. Note items 1 and 3 are the two ways to describe the *same*
physics — that pairing is what makes this a good "all are correct" shape.

questions.text: Precipitation (age) hardening is:

options.label: a
options.text: the strongest of the four mechanisms, and the one behind most high-strength aluminium and many nickel superalloys

options.label: b
options.text: the weakest of the four mechanisms

questions.keyExplanation: Strongest of the four; behind high-strength Al and Ni superalloys.
questions.concise: Precipitation hardening is the strongest of the four.
questions.detailed:
Precipitation (age) hardening gives the largest strengthening increment of the
four classic mechanisms — it is behind high-strength aluminium alloys (2xxx, 7xxx), many nickel
superalloys (γ/γ′ in turbine blades) and age-hardened steels.
- (b) it is the *strongest*, not the weakest.
- (c) it is not a grain-refining treatment (though a heat treatment may do both).
- (d) it goes well beyond a solid-solution effect — the second phase is the point.

questions.text: The three steps of precipitation hardening, in order, are:

options.label: a
options.text: solution treatment (into the single-phase region) → quench (trap a supersaturated solid solution) → age (natural or artificial)

questions.keyExplanation: Solution treat → quench → age. [P2] — memorise the order; it is a common reversal trap.
questions.concise: Solution treat → quench → age. Memorise this order.
questions.detailed:
```
1. Solution treatment: heat into the single-phase region so all solute dissolves
2. Quench: rapid cool to trap a SUPERSATURATED solid solution (no time to precipitate)
3. Age: hold at a moderate T (natural = room T; artificial = elevated T) to let fine,
   controlled precipitates form
```
- (b), (c) reverse the order — **a common reversal trap.** Aging before solution treating makes
  no sense (there is nothing dissolved to age), and quenching first has nothing to trap.
- (d) anneal/temper/normalise are steel heat treatments, not the precipitation sequence.

questions.text: The precipitate evolution sequence, in order of *increasing* size and *decreasing* coherency, is:

options.label: a
options.text: GP zones (fully coherent) → coherent precipitates → semi-coherent → incoherent

questions.keyExplanation: GP zones → coherent → semi-coherent → incoherent (increasing size, decreasing coherency).
questions.concise: GP zones → coherent → semi-coherent → incoherent: increasing size, decreasing coherency.
questions.detailed:
```
GP zones          fully coherent, tiny, coherency strain
→ coherent        still coherent, larger
→ semi-coherent   misfit dislocations appear at the interface
→ incoherent      no coherency, distinct crystal structure, largest
```
As the particles **grow**, the coherency **breaks down** — the lattice mismatch can no longer
be accommodated elastically, so interfacial dislocations appear (semi-coherent), then the
interface becomes completely incoherent.
- (b) is exactly reversed.
- (c), (d) are scrambled.

questions.text: The strength-versus-ageing-time curve shows:

options.label: a
options.text: strength rising through the underaged regime, peaking at optimal precipitate size and spacing, then falling in the overaged regime

questions.keyExplanation: Rise → peak → decline.
questions.concise: Rise → peak → decline (underaged → peak-aged → overaged).
questions.detailed:
```
underaged:   fine, coherent, cutting-dominated  → strength RISING
peak-aged:   optimal size and spacing           → strength MAXIMUM
overaged:    coarse, incoherent, Orowan looping → strength FALLING
```
- (b), (c), (d) all miss the characteristic peak.

The **peak** is the whole point of an ageing treatment — and the reason getting the time/temperature
wrong in *either* direction loses strength (Q38).

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *cutting (shearing)* is/are correct?

statements.text: Small, coherent precipitates can be sheared straight through by a moving dislocation.
Harder precipitates and smaller spacing make cutting progressively more difficult, so strength rises through the underaged regime.
Cutting leaves a loop wrapped around each particle.
Cutting is the mechanism in the overaged condition.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2 correct. Items 3 and 4 describe *Orowan looping*. [P2]
questions.concise: Cutting = small coherent precipitates sheared by the dislocation, rising strength through underaging — items 3 and 4 describe **Orowan looping**.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: small, coherent precipitates can be sheared straight through by a moving
  dislocation (the particle is cut, often creating an anti-phase boundary inside it).
- Item 2 — TRUE: harder precipitates and smaller spacing make cutting progressively more
  difficult, so strength rises through the underaged regime.
- Item 3 — FALSE: leaving a loop wrapped around each particle is **Orowan looping**, not cutting.
- Item 4 — FALSE: cutting is the **underaged** mechanism, not overaged.

Items 3 and 4 belong to the *other* mechanism. **The [P2] test:** *is the dislocation going
through the particle (cutting, underaged) or around it (looping, overaged)?*

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *Orowan looping* is/are correct?

statements.text: Once precipitates coarsen past a critical size (overaging) they become incoherent and too strong to shear.
The dislocation bows between adjacent precipitates, leaving a small loop wrapped around each particle.
Coarsening increases the inter-particle spacing, so the bowing stress needed falls and strength declines past the peak.
Orowan looping occurs in the underaged condition.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — Orowan looping is the *overaged* mechanism. [P2]
questions.concise: Orowan looping = overaged, incoherent particles, bowing between them leaving loops, and coarsening raises spacing so the bowing stress falls.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: once precipitates coarsen past a critical size (overaging) they become
  incoherent and too strong to shear.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the dislocation bows between adjacent precipitates, leaving a small loop
  wrapped around each particle (Orowan looping).
- Item 3 — TRUE: coarsening increases the inter-particle spacing, so the bowing stress needed
  falls — Orowan stress ∝ Gb/λ — and strength declines past the peak.
- Item 4 — FALSE: Orowan looping is the **overaged** mechanism.

Item 4 is the [P2] inversion. The Orowan stress relation is worth having:
```
τ_Orowan ∝ Gb / λ    (λ = inter-particle spacing)
```
Coarsening → λ ↑ → τ ↓ → **weaker**, even though each particle is individually harder.

questions.assertion: Strength declines in the overaged condition even though each individual precipitate is now harder.
questions.reason: Coarsening (Ostwald ripening) also increases the spacing between particles, and the Orowan bowing stress falls as spacing rises.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — spacing, not particle hardness, controls the Orowan stress.
questions.concise: Coarsening increases spacing, and Orowan bowing stress falls as spacing rises — so spacing, not particle hardness, controls strength.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: strength declines in the overaged condition even though each individual precipitate
  is now harder.
- R is TRUE: coarsening (Ostwald ripening) also increases the spacing between particles, and
  the Orowan bowing stress falls as spacing rises.

R correctly explains A. This is the counter-intuitive centrepiece of the chapter:
**the controlling variable is inter-particle spacing, not particle hardness.**
In the overaged condition:
```
particle hardness ↑   BUT   spacing λ ↑↑   →   τ ∝ Gb/λ ↓↓   →   overall strength ↓
```
The spacing effect wins.

questions.text: The classic teaching example of precipitation hardening is the Al–Cu system (2xxx "duralumin"), in which the strengthening phase is:

options.label: a
options.text: θ′ (with GP zones → θ″ → θ′ → θ sequence)

questions.keyExplanation: θ′ in Al–Cu.
questions.concise: Al–Cu duralumin: strengthening phase is θ′, sequence GP → θ″ → θ′ → θ.
questions.detailed:
In the classic Al–Cu (2xxx duralumin) system:
```
supersaturated α  →  GP zones  →  θ″  →  θ′ (peak strength)  →  θ (equilibrium, Al₂Cu)
   coherent            coherent   semi      semi/incoherent      incoherent
```
The **θ′** (theta-prime) is the principal strengthening precipitate at peak ageing.
- (b) cementite Fe₃C is the strengthening phase in **pearlitic steel**, not duralumin.
- (c) martensite is a *diffusionless* transformation product (Ch. 2), not a precipitate.
- (d) α-ferrite is a matrix phase, not a precipitate.

questions.text: Al–Cu duralumin is solution treated around 500 °C, quenched, then aged at room temperature or at a mild artificial-ageing temperature of roughly:
questions.keyExplanation: 150–190 °C artificial ageing.
questions.concise: Artificial ageing of Al–Cu ≈ 150–190 °C.
questions.detailed:
Typical Al–Cu processing:
```
solution treat ~500 °C  →  quench  →  age at room T (natural)
                                    or 150–190 °C (artificial)
```
- (b) 500–600 °C would be solution-treatment (or melting/incipient melting) range, not ageing.
- (c) 20–50 °C is *natural* ageing (room temperature), which is slower.
- (d) 700–800 °C is far too hot — melting territory.

questions.text: Precipitation hardening peaks when:

statements.text: precipitates are just large enough to resist cutting
but not yet coarse enough for easy Orowan looping
getting the ageing treatment wrong in either direction loses strength
precipitates are as coarse as possible

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is the opposite of peak ageing.
questions.concise: Peak = just large enough to resist cutting, not yet coarse enough for easy looping; getting ageing wrong either way loses strength — coarser is NOT better.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: precipitates just large enough to resist cutting.
- Item 2 — TRUE: but not yet coarse enough for easy Orowan looping.
- Item 3 — TRUE: getting the ageing treatment wrong in either direction loses strength
  (underaged → too easy to cut; overaged → too easy to loop).
- Item 4 — FALSE: precipitates "as coarse as possible" describes the *worst* condition — that
  is maximally overaged, with large λ and the lowest Orowan stress.

Item 4 is the false member, and it is the naive "bigger precipitates = more obstruction"
intuition that Q35 explicitly defeats.

questions.text: Match the annealing stage to what happens.
tableRows: (a) new strain-free equiaxed grains nucleate and consume the cold-worked structure
(b) defect annihilation and rearrangement (polygonization); relieves internal stress, no change in grain shape or strength
(c) larger grains consume smaller ones to reduce total grain-boundary energy, lowering strength if overdone
questions.concise: Recovery = defect rearrangement, no grain change · Recrystallisation = new strain-free grains · Grain growth = larger grains consume smaller.
questions.detailed:
| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Recovery** | defect annihilation and rearrangement (polygonisation); relieves internal stress, **no change in grain shape or strength** |
| **Recrystallisation** | new strain-free equiaxed grains nucleate and consume the cold-worked structure → strength drops, ductility restored |
| **Grain growth** | larger grains consume smaller ones to reduce total grain-boundary energy → lowers strength if overdone |

The sequence is fixed: **recovery → recrystallisation → grain growth**, in order of increasing
temperature/time. Each stage is driven by reducing stored energy — first dislocation energy,
then the cold-worked structure itself, then grain-boundary energy.

questions.text: Which factor(s) affect(s) the recrystallisation temperature?

statements.text: Percentage prior cold work — more work → lower T_r
Purity — impurities raise T_r
Initial grain size
The Hall–Petch slope k_y only

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is not a controlling factor.
questions.concise: More prior cold work → lower T_r · impurities → higher T_r · initial grain size all matter; k_y does not control T_r.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: more prior cold work → more stored energy and more nucleation sites → **lower**
  recrystallisation temperature.
- Item 2 — TRUE: impurities pin boundaries and segregate to dislocations → **raise** T_r
  (which is why 99.999% pure metals recrystallise at room temperature).
- Item 3 — TRUE: initial grain size affects the stored energy per unit volume and the boundary
  area available → affects T_r.
- Item 4 — FALSE: the Hall–Petch slope k_y is a *strengthening* parameter (Q14); it is not a
  controlling factor for the recrystallisation temperature.

Item 4 is an unrelated parameter imported from a different equation — the classic P1 "valid
number, wrong context" trap.
